messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Parole Officer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Eye Contact: Making eye contact with other people, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 34-year-old parole officer who came to treatment after months of feeling as if his life had narrowed to vigilance, dread, and the effort of getting through each day without being overwhelmed. He had been in a relationship with a woman who became physically abusive behind closed doors. What he returns to most often is one night after an argument in their apartment, when she cornered him in the kitchen, struck him repeatedly, and shoved him hard enough that he hit the counter and bit the inside of his mouth. He can still summon the metallic, bloody taste from that moment. Later, when he was treated for his injuries, the sharp antiseptic smell of the hospital fixed itself in his mind alongside the sound of her voice during the assault, so that now those sensory details seem fused to the event rather than separate from it.

In the weeks afterward, situations that resembled pieces of the assault began to feel charged with danger. At work, if he passed the medical unit in the courthouse annex and caught the smell of disinfectant, his body would go rigid before he had time to think. If a client’s relative looked at him in a way he experienced as sexualized, or if he found himself alone in a room with another man during a home visit, he became instantly watchful, shoulders tight, eyes moving over exits, hands, posture. He described constantly studying other people for signs they might turn on him. Those same moments also pulled the assault into the present: with the hospital smell in particular, he heard her words in his head as if spoken again, tasted blood in his mouth, and for several seconds lost the sense that it was a memory rather than something happening now. Each trigger also carried a bitter conclusion. Being set off so easily seemed to him proof that what happened had ruined his life, and he would think with anger that it was deeply unfair that she had done this and faced no real consequence.

As these episodes accumulated, Kwame came to believe that he was no longer the man he had been. He said more than once that his life felt destroyed, and on his worst nights he was not sure it was worth living like this. The force of the memories drove those judgments deeper. When the scene came back with her voice in his head and the taste in his mouth, it did not feel like recollection but re-entry, and afterward he took that loss of footing as evidence that the abuse still owned him. The more persistently his body stayed on alert, the more he read that tension as confirmation that the danger had not ended inside him. Even before anything happened in a room, he was already scanning, already braced, and he understood that constant readiness as a sign that the trauma had permanently damaged him.

From there, his efforts to cope began to organize his life. Because he had come to see vulnerability as unsafe and any relief as precarious, he pushed away positive feelings when they appeared, cutting off moments of warmth with his current partner because letting himself feel good seemed like letting his guard down. Because he expected danger in other people, he avoided eye contact, especially in the office waiting area and during field visits, telling himself it was better not to invite attention. Because disagreement had preceded the worst assault, he started avoiding conflict altogether, backing down quickly with coworkers and softening decisions with parolees to prevent any confrontation. These habits made immediate sense to him, but they also kept his body tense and searching. By not looking directly at people, he felt less able to read them and watched them even more covertly. By steering around disagreements, he became more sensitive to any hint that one was emerging. By flattening positive emotion, he lived in a state with little relief from alarm.

Those strategies also seemed to make the memories easier to trigger. In sessions he noticed that when he spent a day avoiding eye contact and swallowing irritation, he was more likely to be thrown by a glance he read as sexual or by being left alone with a man in a conference room. On those days the antiseptic smell from a clinic hallway could bring everything back at full intensity. He had begun to associate whole stretches of his work environment with the possibility of being set off, and that expectation itself made him enter them already braced. The loop had tightened enough that he was pulling back not only from clients and colleagues but from his partner, who told him he was present in body and nowhere else.

What finally brought him in was a recent incident at work when the smell of disinfectant outside an interview room made him hear his ex-partner’s voice so vividly that he had to leave the floor. He sat in his car afterward convinced that nothing would ever change, furious at the unfairness of what had been done to him, and frightened by how often the thought came that maybe life was not worth living if this was all it would be. He is seeking help because he wants the memories to feel past, not present, and because he is afraid that if he keeps living this guarded and hunted, he will lose both his work and the relationship that has so far survived with him.
